monitored_text: Resources / Materials / Cast Iron: Properties, Types and Uses Cast Iron: Properties, Types and Uses Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 42 min read Published November 23, 2026 Cast iron is an iron-carbon alloy with carbon content from 2% to 4% by weight, distinguished from steel by its higher carbon concentration, superior castability, and characteristic microstructure containing graphite or iron carbide phases that determine its mechanical behavior across industrial applications. Cast iron is made of iron (93% to 95%), carbon (2% to 4%), silicon (1% to 3%), manganese (0.25% to 0.75%), phosphorus (below 0.1%), and sulfur (below 0.05%), with silicon playing the critical role of promoting graphite formation during solidification rather than iron carbide (cementite), directly controlling the type of cast iron produced. Cast iron is made by melting pig iron and steel scrap in a cupola or electric induction furnace, adjusting composition through ferroalloy additions, treating the melt with inoculants or magnesium (for ductile iron), and pouring the molten metal into sand, permanent, or die molds where it solidifies into the final shape. The primary types include gray cast iron, white cast iron, ductile cast iron, malleable cast iron, alloy cast iron, and chilled cast iron, each with a distinct microstructure and properties. Key properties include high compressive strength (570 MPa to 1,380 MPa), excellent vibration damping, good wear resistance, and castability into complex geometries. Applications span construction, pipes, cookware, automotive parts, machinery bases, tools, railway components, and architectural elements, establishing cast iron as one of the most widely used engineering materials globally. What Is Cast Iron? Cast iron is an iron-carbon alloy with relatively high carbon content from 2% to 4% by weight, known for hardness, castability, and compressive strength, and widely used in industrial, automotive, construction, and domestic applications where its combination of low cost and adequate mechanical performance makes it the material of choice. The carbon content above 2% exceeds the maximum carbon solubility in austenite at equilibrium (2.14%), causing carbon to precipitate as graphite flakes, graphite nodules, or iron carbide (cementite) during solidification, depending on cooling rate and silicon content. The form of carbon precipitation determines the type of cast iron produced and governs its mechanical behavior: graphite flakes (gray iron) produce a brittle, machinable material; graphite nodules (ductile iron) produce a tough, ductile material; cementite networks (white iron) produce an extremely hard, brittle material. Cast iron is widely used in industrial applications, including engine blocks, pipe systems, machine tool bases, cookware, and structural castings, where its excellent castability into complex near-net-shape geometries reduces machining requirements and manufacturing cost compared to wrought or fabricated alternatives. What Is the Definition of Cast Iron in Materials Engineering? The definition of cast iron in materials engineering is as an iron alloy containing more than 2% carbon by weight, along with silicon from 1% to 3% and minor quantities of manganese, phosphorus, and sulfur, produced by casting molten metal into molds rather than by forging, rolling, or other wrought processing methods. The 2% carbon threshold that defines cast iron in materials engineering corresponds to the maximum carbon solubility in austenite at the eutectic temperature (1,154°C) on the iron-carbon phase diagram; above 2.14%, excess carbon precipitates as a separate phase (graphite or cementite) during solidification, producing the microstructural characteristics that distinguish cast iron from steel. The definition encompasses six primary types (gray, white, ductile, malleable, alloy, and chilled cast iron) that differ in graphite morphology, heat treatment condition, and alloying element additions, all sharing the fundamental characteristic of carbon above 2% and production by the casting process. Cast iron's definition in materials engineering directly predicts its castability, machinability, compressive strength, and brittleness from the compositional and microstructural parameters encoded in the classification. Is Cast Iron an Iron-Carbon Alloy With High Carbon Content? Yes, cast iron is an iron-carbon alloy with high carbon content from 2% to 4% by weight, a concentration that places it at the upper end of the iron-carbon binary system and distinguishes it definitively from steel (carbon 0.008% to 2.14%) and wrought iron (carbon below 0.08%). The high carbon content of cast iron is not a compositional deficiency but a deliberate characteristic that provides castability (carbon depresses the melting point from iron's 1,538°C to the eutectic temperature of 1,154°C), graphite formation (improving machinability and damping), and compressive strength (cementite and pearlite phases resist compressive loading). The carbon range from 2% to 4% defines cast iron's position on the iron-carbon phase diagram, its microstructure type, and its mechanical property profile in every engineering classification system. What Is Cast Iron Made Of? Cast iron is made of iron as the primary constituent (93% to 95% by weight), carbon from 2% to 4%, silicon from 1% to 3%, manganese from 0.25% to 0.75%, phosphorus below 0.1%, and sulfur below 0.05%, with alloying elements including nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and copper added in alloy cast iron grades to modify specific properties. Carbon is the key component that defines cast iron's classification, melting point, and microstructure, while silicon is the secondary element that controls whether carbon precipitates as graphite (high silicon) or iron carbide/cementite (low silicon) during solidification. The silicon content is the primary process variable in cast iron production, with silicon above 1.7% promoting graphite formation in gray iron and silicon below 0.5% promoting white iron cementite microstructure. Manganese combines with sulfur to form MnS, preventing the formation of brittle FeS at grain boundaries, while phosphorus at low levels improves melt fluidity and castability. The composition of cast iron is adjusted during melting to target the specific microstructure and mechanical properties required for the intended application. What Is the Chemical Composition of Cast Iron? The chemical composition of cast iron contains carbon from 2% to 4%, silicon from 1% to 3%, manganese from 0.25% to 0.75%, phosphorus below 0.1%, and sulfur below 0.05%, with iron comprising the balance at approximately 93% to 95% by weight. Silicon controls graphite formation during solidification by reducing the stability of cementite (Fe₃C) and promoting carbon precipitation as graphite, with silicon above 2% producing the graphite-flake microstructure of gray iron. Carbon equivalent (CE), calculated as CE = %C + (%Si + %P)/3, is the primary compositional parameter predicting cast iron solidification behavior, with CE values from 3.9 to 4.4 producing eutectic and hypoeutectic compositions optimal for most gray iron castings. Manganese content from 0.25% to 0.75% neutralizes sulfur by forming MnS, preventing FeS grain boundary films that cause hot tearing during solidification. Phosphorus below 0.1% forms iron phosphide (Fe₃P), a steadite eutectic, which improves fluidity but reduces toughness above 0.1% concentration. Does Cast Iron Contain More Than 2% Carbon? Yes, cast iron contains more than 2% carbon by weight, with the standard compositional range from 2% to 4% carbon establishing it as a hypoeutectic to hypereutectic iron-carbon alloy on the phase diagram. The 2% lower boundary is the defining threshold separating cast iron from steel in materials engineering classification; below 2% carbon, the alloy is steel and forms fully austenitic or ferritic microstructures on solidification without free graphite or excessive cementite. Carbon solubility in austenite is exceeded at carbon levels above 2%, forcing excess carbon to precipitate as graphite or cementite during solidification and producing the microstructure that characterizes cast iron. The iron-carbon phase diagram confirms that 2.14% is the maximum carbon solubility in austenite at the eutectic temperature, making carbon above 2% the universal criterion for cast iron classification in international standards (ASTM A48, ISO 185). How Is Cast Iron Made? Cast iron is made by melting iron raw materials (pig iron, cast iron returns, and steel scrap) in a cupola furnace, electric induction furnace, or electric arc furnace at temperatures from 1,380°C to 1,500°C, adjusting carbon and silicon content through ferroalloy additions, treating the melt for specific microstructure requirements (inoculation for gray iron, magnesium treatment for ductile iron), and pouring the prepared molten metal into sand, permanent metal, or die molds where it solidifies into the near-net-shape final casting. The melting phase combines raw materials to achieve the target composition, with carbon equivalent (CE) measured by thermal analysis or direct spectrometry and adjusted by adding ferrosilicon, carbon raisers, or diluting with steel scrap. The mold design determines the casting geometry, with sand molds enabling the most complex shapes and permanent molds providing better dimensional accuracy and surface finish. Cooling rate within the mold controls microstructure: slow cooling promotes graphite formation (gray iron), while rapid cooling promotes cementite formation (white or chilled iron). Heat treatment after casting (annealing for malleable iron, stress relieving for gray iron) further modifies the microstructure and mechanical properties of the finished casting. What Is the Manufacturing Process of Cast Iron From Molten Iron? The manufacturing process of cast iron from molten iron begins with the melting of iron in a blast furnace or electric arc furnace. Molten iron is refined, alloyed, and poured into molds to form cast iron products through a sequential manufacturing process that begins with charge calculation, proceeds through melting and composition adjustment, and concludes with mold filling, solidification, shakeout, and finishing operations. The charge calculation determines the proportions of pig iron, cast iron returns, steel scrap, and ferroalloys required to achieve the target carbon equivalent and alloy content for the specific cast iron grade. Melting in an induction furnace at 1,400°C to 1,500°C produces a homogeneous melt that is sampled for chemical analysis by optical emission spectrometry, with composition corrections made by ferroalloy additions before tapping. Inoculation (addition of ferrosilicon or graphitizing inoculants just before pouring) refines graphite flake distribution in gray iron, improving mechanical properties and reducing sensitivity to section thickness. The melt is poured at temperatures from 1,320°C to 1,420°C, depending on section thickness and mold type, filling the mold cavity before the metal freezes. Solidification produces the near-net-shape casting with complex geometry, impossible to achieve by forging or machining from solid stock. Is Cast Iron Produced by Pouring Molten Metal Into Molds? Yes, cast iron is produced by pouring molten metal into molds, and the casting process is the defining manufacturing method that gives cast iron its name and its primary advantage over wrought iron and steel in producing complex, near-net-shape components. Sand casting, the most common method, uses expendable bonded sand molds that allow essentially unlimited geometric complexity, including internal passages, undercuts, and variable wall thickness from 3 mm to over 200 mm. Permanent mold casting and die casting produce cast iron components with tighter dimensional tolerances (±0.25 mm to ±0.5 mm) and better surface finish (Ra 3.2 µm to Ra 6.3 µm) than sand casting. The mold filling and solidification during the casting process fix the part geometry, with machining limited to functional surfaces requiring dimensional accuracy or surface finish below Ra 1.6 µm. Casting as the production method distinguishes cast iron from wrought ferrous metals and defines its manufacturing cost advantage for complex geometry components. What Are the Main Properties of Cast Iron? The main properties of cast iron are listed below. Compressive Strength : Cast iron has compressive strength from 570 MPa to 1,380 MPa, depending on grade, significantly exceeding its tensile strength and making it well-suited for structural applications dominated by compressive loading (columns, machine bases, pipe fittings). Tensile Strength : Gray cast iron tensile strength ranges from 100 MPa to 400 MPa, while ductile iron reaches 414 MPa to 827 MPa. The tensile strength limitation of gray iron arises from graphite flakes that act as stress concentrators under tensile loading. Hardness : Cast iron hardness ranges from 150 HB to 700 HB, depending on grade and heat treatment. Gray iron falls from 150 HB to 300 HB, white iron from 400 HB to 700 HB, and ductile iron from 140 HB to 300 HB. Vibration Damping : Gray cast iron has a vibration-damping capacity approximately 10 times greater than that of structural steel, due to graphite flakes that absorb and dissipate mechanical vibration energy. The damping property makes gray iron the standard material for machine tool bases and engine blocks. Castability : Cast iron's carbon content depresses the melting point to 1,150°C to 1,200°C and reduces liquid viscosity, producing excellent flow into complex mold cavities with section thicknesses from 3 mm to over 200 mm. Wear Resistance : The graphite in the cast iron microstructure acts as a self-lubricating agent, reducing friction at sliding surfaces. Wear resistance values from 0.1 mm³/Nm to 0.5 mm³/Nm (pin-on-disk testing) are typical for gray and white cast iron grades. Machinability : Gray cast iron machines at cutting speeds from 90 m/min to 180 m/min with carbide tooling, faster than most steels, due to graphite flakes that act as chip breakers and lubricants at the tool-chip interface. How Do Carbon and Graphite Affect Cast Iron Properties? Carbon and graphite affect cast iron properties by influencing its strength, hardness, and machinability. Carbon and graphite in cast iron determine the material's tensile strength, ductility, hardness, machinability, damping capacity, and wear resistance through the form, size, and distribution of carbon-containing phases in the microstructure. In gray cast iron, carbon precipitates as graphite flakes during solidification; the flakes act as stress concentrators that limit tensile strength to 100 MPa to 400 MPa but simultaneously provide crack-arresting interfaces that improve vibration damping (10 times greater than steel), self-lubrication at sliding surfaces, and chip-breaking action during machining. In ductile cast iron, magnesium treatment converts graphite from flakes to nodules, eliminating the stress concentration effect and increasing tensile strength to 414 MPa to 827 MPa and elongation to 10% to 18%. Carbon remains as cementite (Fe₃C) rather than precipitating as graphite in white cast iron, producing hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB with near-zero ductility. The carbon-graphite relationship in cast iron confirms that the form of carbon precipitation, instead of total carbon content alone, is the primary determinant of mechanical properties in the four principal cast iron types. Is Cast Iron Brittle Compared to Steel? Yes, cast iron is more brittle than steel in most grades, with gray cast iron exhibiting elongation at fracture below 1% and Charpy impact energy below 5 J, compared to mild steel elongation from 18% to 25% and impact energy from 27 J to over 100 J. The brittleness of gray cast iron arises from graphite flakes that act as pre-existing crack-like defects, concentrating tensile stress and initiating fracture at low applied loads. White cast iron is the most brittle cast iron grade, with elongation near 0% due to continuous cementite networks that provide no plastic deformation mechanism. Ductile cast iron is the exception; magnesium-induced nodular graphite eliminates the stress concentration effect, producing elongation from 10% to 18%, comparable to lower-strength steel grades. The brittleness comparison from cast iron to steel explains why cast iron is designed for compressive-load applications and why ductile iron was developed to address the toughness limitations of gray iron in tensile and impact-loaded service environments. What Are the Different Types of Cast Iron? The different types of cast iron are shown in the table below. The Types of Cast Iron are differentiated primarily by graphite morphology (form of carbon precipitation), silicon content (controlling graphite vs. cementite formation), and heat treatment condition, each producing a distinct combination of mechanical properties suited to specific engineering applications. 1. Gray Cast Iron Gray cast iron is the most widely produced cast iron grade, characterized by graphite flakes distributed throughout a pearlitic or ferritic iron matrix, producing a material with tensile strength from 100 MPa to 400 MPa, hardness from 150 HB to 300 HB, and the highest vibration-damping capacity of any common engineering metal. The graphite flakes in gray iron give a fractured surface a gray color (from which the grade takes its name) and act simultaneously as stress concentrators in tension (limiting tensile strength) and as vibration absorbers (providing damping 10 times greater than steel). Gray iron is classified by ASTM A48 into classes (20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60) based on minimum tensile strength in ksi, with Class 20 (138 MPa) representing the most machinable grade and Class 60 (414 MPa) the highest strength. The excellent machinability of gray iron (cutting speeds from 90 m/min to 180 m/min with carbide tooling), low cost, and complex castability make it the default material for engine blocks, cylinder heads, machine tool bases, brake rotors, and pipe systems. Xometry's casting services produce Grey Cast Iron components across ASTM A48 classes for automotive, industrial, and infrastructure applications. 2. White Cast Iron White cast iron is produced when molten cast iron solidifies rapidly or with low silicon content (below 1%), preventing graphite formation and causing all carbon to remain as iron carbide (cementite, Fe₃C) in a ledeburite matrix, producing a material with extreme hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB and near-zero ductility (elongation below 0.5%). The fractured surface of white cast iron appears white and crystalline due to the reflective cementite phase, contrasting with the gray graphite-containing surface of gray iron. White cast iron's extreme hardness and wear resistance make it the standard material for applications requiring abrasion resistance: ball mill liners, slurry pump impellers, crusher wear plates, and shot blast equipment components where softer materials would wear rapidly. White cast iron is essentially unweldable and unmachineable by conventional cutting tools due to its hardness; components are produced in their final shape by casting and grinding with diamond wheels. White iron is also the precursor material for malleable iron production, where extended annealing heat treatment converts cementite to tempered carbon clusters. 3. Ductile Cast Iron (Nodular Cast Iron) Ductile cast iron, also called nodular cast iron or spheroidal graphite iron, is produced by treating molten gray iron with 0.03% to 0.05% magnesium (added as magnesium ferrosilicon or pure magnesium wire) immediately before casting, which transforms graphite morphology from flakes to spherical nodules during solidification. The nodular graphite eliminates the stress concentration effect of graphite flakes, producing tensile strength from 414 MPa to 827 MPa, yield strength from 276 MPa to 621 MPa, and elongation from 10% to 18%, with mechanical properties comparable to cast carbon steel at substantially lower cost. ASTM A536 classifies ductile iron into grades (60-40-18, 65-45-12, 80-55-06, 100-70-03, 120-90-02) where the three numbers represent minimum tensile strength (ksi), yield strength (ksi), and elongation (%). Ductile iron's combination of strength, ductility, machinability, and castability makes it the preferred material for crankshafts, differential housings, steering knuckles, gears, heavy truck components, and ductile iron pressure pipe (AWWA C151) in municipal water distribution systems. Xometry's manufacturing services cover Ductile Cast Iron components for automotive, agricultural, and infrastructure applications requiring higher toughness than gray iron provides. 4. Malleable Cast Iron Malleable cast iron is produced by annealing white cast iron castings at 900°C to 970°C for 15 to 20 hours, followed by slow cooling, which converts the brittle cementite (Fe₃C) microstructure into clusters of temper carbon (irregular graphite nodules) in a ferritic or pearlitic matrix, producing tensile strength from 345 MPa to 550 MPa and elongation from 5% to 12%. The annealing process requires precise temperature control to fully decompose cementite without remelting or oxidizing the casting, and the extended cycle time (up to 80 hours for thick sections) adds processing cost relative to gray iron but produces a material with substantially better ductility for thin-section complex castings. Malleable cast iron is classified by ASTM A47 into ferritic grades (32510: 345 MPa tensile, 224 MPa yield, 10% elongation) and ASTM A220 pearlitic grades (higher strength, lower ductility). Applications include pipe fittings, electrical conduit fittings, agricultural implement components, and hand tool hardware where moderate ductility in thin-walled complex castings is required. Xometry's casting network produces Malleable Cast Iron components for fitting, hardware, and tool applications. 5. Alloy Cast Iron Alloy cast iron is produced by adding alloying elements including nickel (up to 36%), chromium (up to 28%), molybdenum (up to 3%), copper (up to 8%), and silicon (up to 18%) to the base gray or white iron composition to achieve specific corrosion resistance, heat resistance, or wear resistance properties not available in unalloyed cast iron grades. Ni-Resist austenitic cast iron (13% to 36% Ni) maintains austenitic microstructure at room temperature, providing corrosion resistance to seawater, alkalis, and organic acids, with tensile strength from 170 MPa to 270 MPa and good toughness at cryogenic temperatures. High-chromium white cast iron (12% to 28% Cr) produces hard chromium carbides (Cr₇C₃, Cr₂₃C₆) with hardness from 55 HRC to 67 HRC for severe abrasion applications in slurry pumps, coal pulverizer parts, and mining equipment. High-silicon cast iron (14% to 16% Si, Duriron) resists concentrated sulfuric and nitric acid at concentrations from 10% to 100%, used in chemical plant piping and reactor components. Xometry's specialty casting services include Alloy Cast Iron grades for corrosive, high-temperature, and extreme wear service environments. 6. Chilled Cast Iron Chilled cast iron is produced by accelerating the cooling rate at selected surfaces of a casting through contact with metal chills (cast iron or steel inserts) placed in the sand mold at critical wear locations, converting those surface regions from graphitic gray iron to hard white iron (cementite microstructure) while the interior cools more slowly and retains a tougher gray iron core. The chilled surface layer achieves hardness from 400 HB to 700 HB and white iron microstructure to a depth from 5 mm to 25 mm, depending on chill size and thermal contact efficiency, while the gray iron core maintains toughness sufficient to resist fracture under impact and bending loads. Railcar wheels in chilled cast iron were among the earliest applications, with the tread and flange surfaces chilled for wear resistance against rail contact, while the wheel plate and hub remained gray iron for impact toughness. Camshafts, plow shares, and rolling mill rolls are produced in chilled cast iron to exploit the hard wear-resistant surface with tough interior core combination that neither pure gray iron nor pure white iron provides individually. What Is the Difference Between Cast Iron and Wrought Iron? The difference between cast iron and wrought iron is shown in the table below. The comparison from cast iron to Wrought Iron reflects the fundamental difference from high-carbon brittle casting material to low-carbon ductile wrought material, two endpoints of the ferrous metals family connected only by iron as the common base element. How Does Cast Iron Compare to Steel? Cast iron compares to steel as a harder, more brittle, more castable, and lower-cost material for compressive and complex-geometry applications, while steel offers superior tensile strength, ductility, toughness, and weldability for structural and dynamic loading applications. Cast iron contains carbon from 2% to 4%, producing graphite or cementite phases that limit tensile strength (100 MPa to 400 MPa in gray iron) but provide compressive strength (570 MPa to 1,380 MPa), vibration damping (10 times greater than steel), and machinability advantages. Steel contains carbon from 0.008% to 2.14%, forming ferritic, pearlitic, martensitic, or austenitic microstructures with tensile strength from 400 MPa to over 2,000 MPa, elongation from 10% to 35%, and full weldability across standard grades. Cast iron costs less to produce than steel for complex-geometry components because the casting process achieves near-net shape without the extensive machining, forging, and forming operations required to produce equivalent geometry in steel, making cast iron the preferred material where compressive strength, vibration damping, and complex castability outweigh the tensile strength and ductility advantages of steel. Is Cast Iron Harder but Less Ductile Than Wrought Iron? Yes, cast iron is harder but less ductile than wrought iron, with gray cast iron hardness from 150 HB to 300 HB exceeding wrought iron's 100 HB to 130 HB, while gray iron elongation below 1% falls far short of wrought iron's 20% to 35% elongation at fracture. The hardness advantage of cast iron arises from pearlite, cementite, and graphite phases in the microstructure that resist indentation more effectively than wrought iron's near-pure ferritic matrix. The ductility disadvantage of cast iron results from graphite flakes (gray iron) or cementite networks (white iron) that provide crack initiation sites, eliminating plastic deformation before fracture. Ductile cast iron partially bridges the gap from cast iron to wrought iron in ductility, achieving elongation from 10% to 18% through nodular graphite formation, but wrought iron's 20% to 35% elongation and superior fatigue resistance from slag fiber reinforcement retain the ductility advantage in ferrous materials comparison. How Does Cast Iron Compare to Ductile Materials? Cast iron compares to most ductile materials in tensile toughness, impact resistance, and elongation at fracture, as gray cast iron's graphite flake microstructure limits elongation to below 1% and Charpy impact energy to below 5 J, properties far below those of ductile materials including mild steel (elongation 18% to 25%, impact energy 27 J to over 100 J), aluminum alloys (elongation 10% to 25%), and engineering plastics (elongation 50% to 300%). The brittleness of gray cast iron arises from the fundamental microstructural characteristic that defines it: graphite flakes act as pre-existing notches that concentrate tensile stress and initiate fracture at low applied strain levels. Ductile cast iron (nodular iron) represents the cast iron grade engineered specifically to approach the properties of ductile materials, achieving elongation from 10% to 18% and impact energy from 7 J to over 100 J (at room temperature, grade-dependent), making it suitable for applications requiring moderate ductility combined with cast iron's manufacturing and cost advantages. Xometry's material selection guidance covers the full spectrum of ductile materials alongside cast iron for applications where the optimal combination of castability, strength, and deformation capacity must be evaluated. Why Is Cast Iron Less Flexible Than Most Ductile Materials? Cast iron is less flexible than most ductile materials because graphite flakes in gray iron (and cementite networks in white iron) act as pre-existing microstructural defects that initiate brittle fracture at low applied strain levels, preventing the plastic deformation mechanisms (dislocation movement, grain boundary sliding, twin formation) that allow ductile materials to deform extensively before failure. In gray cast iron, graphite flakes with aspect ratios from 10:1 to 100:1 concentrate tensile stress at their tips by factors of 10 to 100 times the nominal applied stress, initiating cracks at strain levels of 0.05% to 0.1%, well below the 1% to 5% strain at which ductile metals begin significant plastic deformation. The absence of effective crack-arresting mechanisms in gray iron's brittle pearlitic matrix means cracks initiated at graphite flake tips propagate rapidly to fracture without the energy-absorbing plastic deformation that makes ductile materials flexible under load. Is Cast Iron Considered a Brittle Material Instead of a Ductile One? Yes, cast iron is considered a brittle material instead of a ductile one in materials engineering, exhibiting elongation at fracture below 1%, no significant yield point before fracture, and fracture surfaces showing cleavage or mixed-mode fracture rather than the necking and shear lip characteristic of ductile failure. The brittle classification applies specifically to gray and white iron; ductile cast iron (nodular iron) is not classified as brittle, achieving elongation from 10% to 18% and behavior on tensile test stress-strain curves that shows a defined yield point and plastic deformation region before fracture. Malleable cast iron occupies an intermediate position, with elongation from 5% to 12% that places it at the boundary from brittle to marginally ductile behavior. The brittle classification of gray cast iron restricts its use in tensile and impact-loaded applications and confirms the need for ductile iron or steel in structural members subjected to dynamic, shock, or tensile loading conditions. What Base Metals Are Used in the Production of Cast Iron? The base metals used in the production of cast iron are listed below. Iron (Fe) : Iron is the primary constituent of cast iron at 93% to 95% by weight, providing the metallic matrix in which all other elements dissolve or precipitate. The purity and consistency of the iron charge directly determine the final mechanical properties and microstructure of the cast iron produced. Carbon (C) : Carbon at 2% to 4% is the defining alloying element of cast iron, controlling microstructure type (graphite vs. cementite), melting point depression, and mechanical properties, including hardness, brittleness, and machinability. Silicon (Si) : Silicon at 1% to 3% is the graphitization promoter in cast iron, thermodynamically stabilizing graphite over cementite during solidification. Silicon content is the primary variable determining whether gray or white iron microstructure forms at a given cooling rate. Manganese (Mn) : Manganese at 0.25% to 0.75% combines with sulfur to form MnS, preventing the formation of brittle FeS grain boundary films. Manganese also stabilizes pearlite in the iron matrix, improving tensile strength and hardness. Sulfur (S) : Sulfur below 0.05% is controlled as an impurity in most cast iron grades; excess sulfur promotes FeS formation that reduces fluidity and causes hot tearing during solidification. Sulfur is managed by maintaining adequate manganese content at a Mn:S ratio above 4:1. Phosphorus (P) : Phosphorus below 0.1% forms iron phosphide steadite (Fe₃P eutectic) that improves melt fluidity and castability for thin-section components but reduces toughness and machinability above 0.1% concentration. 1. Iron (Fe) Iron is the foundational base metal in cast iron production, constituting approximately 93% to 95% of the total composition and providing the metallic matrix within which carbon, silicon, manganese, and other elements dissolve or precipitate to form the microstructure. The iron used in cast iron production enters the process as pig iron (from blast furnace reduction of iron ore), cast iron returns (remelted sprues, runners, and scrap castings), and steel scrap (for diluting carbon and adjusting composition). Iron's crystal structure transitions from BCC (ferrite, below 912°C) to FCC (austenite, 912°C to 1,394°C) and back to BCC (delta iron, 1,394°C to 1,538°C) during heating and cooling, with these phase transformations governing the microstructure evolution during cast iron solidification and subsequent heat treatment. The charge calculation for cast iron production begins with Iron (Fe) as the reference constituent, with all other elements calculated relative to the iron base to achieve the target carbon equivalent and microstructure. 2. Carbon (C) Carbon at 2% to 4% by weight is the defining element in cast iron, separating it from steel (carbon below 2.14%) and controlling the microstructure, melting point, castability, hardness, and mechanical behavior of every cast iron grade produced. Carbon reduces the melting point of the iron-carbon alloy from pure iron's 1,538°C to the eutectic temperature of 1,154°C at 4.3% carbon, improving fluidity and castability of the liquid metal. Carbon precipitates during solidification either as graphite (stable phase, promoted by silicon and slow cooling) or as cementite (metastable phase, promoted by rapid cooling and low silicon), with the precipitation form governing all subsequent mechanical properties. The Carbon (C) content range from 2% to 4% places cast iron in the hypoeutectic to hypereutectic region of the iron-carbon phase diagram, producing the eutectic graphite and primary phases that characterize cast iron microstructure. 3. Silicon (Si) Silicon at 1% to 3% by weight in cast iron acts as the primary graphitization promoter, thermodynamically destabilizing iron carbide (cementite, Fe₃C) and driving carbon to precipitate as graphite during solidification, determining whether the cast iron solidifies as gray iron (graphite flakes), white iron (cementite), or an intermediate structure depending on silicon level and cooling rate. Graphite formation is strongly favored at all practical cooling rates at silicon above 2%, producing gray iron with graphite flakes in most section thicknesses from 5 mm to 100 mm. At silicon below 1%, cementite formation is promoted, producing white iron at normal sand casting cooling rates. The microstructure is section-sensitive at silicon from 1% to 2%, with thin sections forming white iron and thick sections forming gray iron in the same casting. The Silicon (Si) content is the primary composition variable adjusted by foundry engineers to control the gray/white iron balance in production castings. 4. Manganese (Mn) Manganese at 0.25% to 0.75% in cast iron performs two primary metallurgical functions: neutralizing sulfur impurity by forming MnS inclusions, and stabilizing the pearlite phase in the iron matrix to improve tensile strength and hardness. The Mn:S ratio is maintained above 4:1 in quality gray iron production to ensure complete sulfur neutralization by manganese. Sulfur enters the cast iron melt from pig iron (typically 0.02% to 0.05% S), steel scrap (below 0.05%), and coke combustion in cupola furnaces (up to 0.12% S pickup from cupola coke). sections.heading: What Is Cast Iron?
sections.text: What Is Cast Iron? Cast iron is an iron-carbon alloy with relatively high carbon content from 2% to 4% by weight, known for hardness, castability, and compressive strength, and widely used in industrial, automotive, construction, and domestic applications where its combination of low cost and adequate mechanical performance makes it the material of choice. sections.text: What Is the Definition of Cast Iron in Materials Engineering? The definition of cast iron in materials engineering is as an iron alloy containing more than 2% carbon by weight, along with silicon from 1% to 3% and minor quantities of manganese, phosphorus, and sulfur, produced by casting molten metal into molds rather than by forging, rolling, or other wrought processing methods. The definition encompasses six primary types (gray, white, ductile, malleable, alloy, and chilled cast iron) that differ in graphite morphology, heat treatment condition, and alloying element additions, all sharing the fundamental characteristic of carbon above 2% and production by the casting process. sections.text: What Makes Cast Iron and Carbon Steel Structurally Different? Cast iron and carbon steel are structurally different because cast iron contains free carbon phases (graphite or cementite) distributed throughout the iron matrix as a result of carbon exceeding solubility limits, while carbon steel contains carbon fully dissolved in the iron lattice in solid solution or as fine carbide precipitates without free graphite or coarse cementite networks at room temperature. The graphite flakes in gray cast iron create a discontinuous matrix where graphite occupies 6% to 10% of the microstructure volume, acting as pre-existing crack-like defects that eliminate plastic deformation capacity in tension. Carbon steel's homogeneous ferritic, pearlitic, or martensitic microstructure contains no free graphite, producing a continuous metal matrix with uniform mechanical properties in all directions. The structural difference from cast iron to carbon steel explains why cast iron excels in compression and vibration-damping applications while carbon steel dominates tensile-loaded structural and mechanical engineering applications where carbon steel's weldability, ductility, and toughness are required....

sections.heading: 1. Construction and Structural Components (Columns, Beams, Manhole Covers)
sections.text: 1. Construction and Structural Components (Columns, Beams, Manhole Covers) Cast iron construction and structural components were the dominant structural metal in buildings and bridges from the late 18th century through the mid-19th century, with the material's high compressive strength (570 MPa to 1,380 MPa) and complex castability enabling column, beam, and connection designs impossible in wrought iron or timber at equivalent cost. Cast iron columns in historic mill buildings and civic structures carry compressive loads from 500 kN to over 5,000 kN per column, with hollow cylindrical sections from 150 mm to 600 mm outside diameter providing efficient compressive load paths at lower weight than solid sections. Cast iron manhole covers and drainage frames are produced to EN 124 and ASTM A48 specifications in gray iron and ductile iron, with load ratings from Group A (1.5 metric tons, pedestrian areas) to Group F (90 metric tons, aircraft pavement), exploiting cast iron's compressive strength and complex-geometry castability for covers with drainage patterns, text, and interlocking features formed in a single casting operation. sections.heading: 2. Pipes and Plumbing Systems (Water and Sewage Pipes)
sections.text: 2. Pipes and Plumbing Systems (Water and Sewage Pipes) Cast iron pipes have supplied municipal water, sewage, and gas distribution infrastructure since the 17th century, with gray iron pipes installed in Paris and London water systems from the 1660s still in service in some networks, demonstrating the material's exceptional service life in underground corrosive environments. Modern cast iron pipe production is dominated by centrifugally cast ductile iron (spheroidal graphite iron) manufactured to AWWA C151 (American Water Works Association) specifications, with pipe diameters from 100 mm to 1,600 mm and pressure ratings from 1,380 kPa to 2,400 kPa for water distribution mains. Ductile iron pipe's tensile strength from 414 MPa to 483 MPa and elongation from 10% to 18% provide the structural integrity to withstand soil loading, water hammer pressure transients, and installation forces from thrust blocks and pipe joints. sections.heading: 3. Cookware (Pots, Pans, Skillets, Dutch Ovens)
sections.text: 3. Cookware (Pots, Pans, Skillets, Dutch Ovens) Cast iron cookware exploits the material's high volumetric heat capacity (approximately 3.5 MJ/(m³·K)), excellent thermal mass, and ability to maintain elevated and stable cooking temperatures for even heat distribution, high-temperature searing, and long slow-cooking applications where temperature consistency determines food quality outcomes. Cast iron skillets, Dutch ovens, griddles, and pots are produced by sand casting gray iron with 3% to 3.5% carbon and 1.8% to 2.2% silicon, producing a dense, pore-free casting after careful mold design and gating to prevent shrinkage defects. Cast iron cookware heats slowly compared to aluminum or copper cookware due to its lower thermal conductivity (50 W/(m·K) versus copper's 400 W/(m·K)), but retains heat far longer after removal from the heat source, making it preferred for applications requiring sustained high temperatures, including bread baking, deep frying, and campfire cooking. sections.heading: 4. Automotive Parts (Engine Blocks, Brake Components)
sections.text: 4. Automotive Parts (Engine Blocks, Brake Components) Cast iron remains the dominant material for engine blocks, cylinder heads, brake rotors, brake drums, and exhaust manifolds in automotive applications, exploiting gray iron's vibration damping (10 times greater than steel), thermal stability (maintaining strength to 300°C to 500°C), wear resistance at cylinder bore surfaces, and cost-effective castability of complex internal geometries including water jacket passages, oil galleries, and bearing housings. Gray iron engine blocks (ASTM A48 Class 30 to Class 40) in passenger vehicles contain cylinder bores with surface hardness from 180 HB to 240 HB after machining and honing, providing wear-resistant cylinder walls for piston ring contact without separate liner inserts in most applications. Compacted graphite iron (CGI) is used in high-performance diesel engine blocks, providing tensile strength from 300 MPa to 450 MPa (50% to 75% above gray iron) and fatigue strength 100% greater than gray iron at a weight saving of 10% to 20% compared to conventional gray iron blocks. sections.heading: 5. Machinery Bases and Frames (Industrial Machines, Heavy Equipment)
sections.text: 5. Machinery Bases and Frames (Industrial Machines, Heavy Equipment) Cast iron machinery bases, lathe beds, milling machine columns, grinding machine tables, and press frames exploit gray iron's vibration-damping capacity (approximately 10 times greater than structural steel) to reduce tool chatter, improve surface finish quality in machining operations, and extend cutting tool life in precision machine tool applications. Machine tool castings in gray iron (ASTM A48 Class 40 to Class 60) weigh from 500 kg to over 50,000 kg per casting, providing the combination of high mass and high damping coefficient required for precision grinding, turning, and milling at cutting speeds from 50 m/min to 500 m/min. The stress-relief annealing of machine tool castings at 500°C to 600°C for 1 hour per 25 mm of section thickness removes residual stresses from the casting process that would cause dimensional drift during precision machining operations over the machine tool's service life. sections.heading: 6. Tools and Agricultural Equipment
sections.text: 6. Tools and Agricultural Equipment Cast iron tools and agricultural equipment exploit the material's high compressive strength, wear resistance, and low-cost castability for vises, anvils, pipe clamps, planer tables, drill press columns, plow shares, harrow discs, and implement frames where static loading and abrasive wear are the primary service conditions. Machinist vises in gray cast iron (ASTM A48 Class 30 to Class 40) provide jaw clamping forces from 5 kN to 50 kN without permanent deformation, relying on cast iron's compressive strength of 570 MPa to 700 MPa at the jaw and screw contact surfaces. Agricultural plow shares and tillage points in white iron or chilled gray iron achieve surface hardness from 400 HB to 600 HB that resists abrasion from soil contact, sand particles, and rock fragments encountered during field operations, with service lives from 50 hours to 200 hours of tillage depending on soil abrasivity and share grade. Cast iron harrow discs in alloy white iron containing 2% to 3% chromium provide improved wear life from 30% to 50% above unalloyed white iron in highly abrasive sandy soils.

sections.heading: 7. Railway Components (Brake Shoes, Fittings)
sections.text: 7. Railway Components (Brake Shoes, Fittings) Cast iron railway brake shoes, bogie frames, wheel castings, and track fittings have been standard components in rail transportation since the earliest railway systems of the 19th century, exploiting gray iron's wear resistance, thermal stability, and compressive strength for components subjected to repeated friction, thermal cycling, and heavy static loads. Cast iron brake shoes generate friction forces against steel wheel treads during braking, with the shoe material selected to produce a coefficient of friction from 0.15 to 0.30 (lower than organic composite shoes) for predictable braking force modulation at wheel-shoe contact pressures from 0.5 MPa to 1.5 MPa. The thermal mass of cast iron brake shoes absorbs braking energy during emergency stops without reaching temperatures that cause structural failure or wheel tread damage, with surface temperatures at the shoe-wheel interface reaching 400°C to 600°C during heavy braking events. sections.heading: 8. Decorative and Architectural Elements (Railings, Gates, Fixtures)
sections.text: 8. Decorative and Architectural Elements (Railings, Gates, Fixtures) Cast iron decorative and architectural components, including railings, gates, lamp posts, balcony balustrades, stair newel posts, building facades, and ornamental fixtures, exploit the material's exceptional castability into complex ornamental geometries that would require prohibitive labor to fabricate from wrought or welded steel. Victorian-era cast iron architectural components (1837 to 1901) include some of the most intricate decorative ironwork ever produced, with gothic tracery, naturalistic foliage, and figurative elements cast in gray iron using hand-carved wooden patterns, producing details with dimensional resolution below 1 mm. Cast iron lamp posts in municipal streetscapes carry vertical loads from 200 kg to 500 kg (luminaire and arm weight plus wind loading) and are designed as hollow tapered columns from 75 mm to 150 mm base diameter, produced by pit casting or horizontal permanent mold casting in gray iron at wall thicknesses from 10 mm to 20 mm. sections.heading: What Are the Advantages of Using Cast Iron?
sections.text: What Are the Advantages of Using Cast Iron? The advantages of using cast iron are listed below. Excellent Castability : Cast iron's carbon-depressed melting point (1,150°C to 1,200°C) and low liquid viscosity allow filling of complex mold cavities with section thicknesses from 3 mm to over 200 mm, producing near-net-shape components with internal passages, undercuts, and complex geometry at lower cost than machining from solid stock. High Compressive Strength : Gray iron compressive strength from 570 MPa to 1,380 MPa, substantially exceeding its tensile strength, makes cast iron ideal for columns, machine bases, pipes, and structural components primarily loaded in compression. Superior Vibration Damping : Gray cast iron absorbs and dissipates mechanical vibration energy approximately 10 times more effectively than structural steel due to graphite flake energy absorption, reducing noise, chatter, and fatigue damage in machine tool bases, engine blocks, and rotating machinery housings.
